title: How to Find a Competitor's Ad Landing Pages (2026)
summary: How to find every landing page a competitor sends ad traffic to: Meta Ad Library links, UTMs, ad libraries, what to look for and how to log what you find.
body_markdown:
## The short answer


- Open the competitor's ads in an ad library, click each ad's call-to-action button, and note the page it lands on. That page is the landing page.
- Do it for every active ad, not a sample. Competitors often run one ad per landing page, so the list of destinations is the list of offers they are testing.
- Read the URL after the click. UTM tags such as` utm_campaign` often name the campaign, audience or creative.
- Landing pages that appear in many ads or have run for months are the ones to study. A new page on one ad is a test.
- The[Sprites ads library](https://www.sprites.ai/ads-library) lists destinations on a brand's page so you can skip the clicking.


An ad is a promise, and the landing page is where the competitor keeps it. Looking at the ad alone tells you the hook. Looking at the page tells you the offer, the price, the proof and what the visitor is asked to do. Here is how to collect the pages for any brand, and what to do with them.


## Why the landing page matters more than the ad


Ad copy is written to earn a click. The landing page is written to earn the sale or the lead, and it is where a competitor's real positioning shows. You will see the price they dare to show, the guarantee, the testimonials, the form length and whether they push a call, a demo, a trial or a purchase.


It also tells you how mature a competitor's funnel is. A brand that sends every ad to its homepage is still guessing. One that sends each ad to a page matched to its message has done the work, and is worth copying from.


## Method 1: Meta Ad Library, ad by ad


1. **Open the library and search the brand.** Go to the Meta Ad Library, choose All ads, and search by the brand's Page name. Pick the Page, not a keyword result.
2. **Set the filters.** Filter to active ads and the country you care about. Filters change what you see, and a competitor's US ads can differ from its UK ads.
3. **Find the call-to-action button.** Most ads show a button such as Shop now or Learn more, and a small line of text with the destination domain.
4. **Click through.** The button opens the page. Open it in a private window so your own cookies do not change what you see.
5. **Copy the final address.** Paste the full URL, with everything after the question mark, into a sheet. Do not trim it.


The full walk-through of the library itself is in[how to see competitors' Facebook ads](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/how-to-see-competitors-facebook-ads) .


## Method 2: Read the UTM tags


Many advertisers tag their links so their own analytics can tell campaigns apart. When you click an ad and look at the address, you will often see parameters like these:


Parameter What it usually tells you


` utm_source` Where the click came from, such as facebook or instagram.


` utm_medium` The channel type, such as paid social or cpc.


` utm_campaign` A campaign name. Often reveals the offer, the season or the audience.


` utm_content` The ad or creative variant. Shows what they are split testing.


` utm_term` A keyword, mostly on search ads.


These names are chosen by the competitor and can be sloppy, coded or empty. Treat them as clues. A campaign called` bf-bundle-25off` tells you a Black Friday bundle at a discount. One called` cmp_4482` tells you nothing, but still tells you the ad and the page belong together.


To understand how these links are built, and to tag your own properly, the[UTM builder](https://www.sprites.ai/tools/utm-builder) shows the structure.


## Method 3: An ad library that lists destinations


Clicking fifty ads is slow. A brand page in an ad library can show the destinations next to the creatives, so you read the list instead of making it.


On Sprites, brand pages live at` /{brand}-ads` , for example[Nike ads](https://www.sprites.ai/nike-ads) and[Canva ads](https://www.sprites.ai/canva-ads) . Category pages group a whole market, such as[ecommerce ads](https://www.sprites.ai/ecommerce-ads) and[SaaS ads](https://www.sprites.ai/saas-ads) , so you can compare where several competitors send traffic. They are free to read.


## Method 4: Search, TikTok and other channels


- **Google search ads.** Google's Ads Transparency Center lists an advertiser's ads. Search the brand's own keywords and click their ad to see its page. Doing so costs the advertiser a click, so do it sparingly.
- **TikTok.** TikTok's Creative Center and the EU Commercial Content Library show ads and sometimes their destinations. See the guides to the[TikTok Creative Center](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/tiktok-creative-center-guide) and[tracking TikTok competitors](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/track-tiktok-competitors-without-following) .
- **LinkedIn.** The LinkedIn Ad Library lists a company's ads, and each shows its link on click.


## What to look for on each page


1. **Message match.** Does the headline repeat the ad's promise? A match means they tested for it.
2. **The offer.** Price, trial, discount, guarantee, bundle. Write it down exactly.
3. **The single action.** One button repeated, or a menu full of distractions? Dedicated pages usually strip the navigation.
4. **Proof.** Reviews, logos, numbers, press, before and after. Note what kind and where it sits.
5. **Form or checkout length.** Count the fields. Lead forms with three fields and ones with ten are different bets.
6. **Page type.** Product page, collection, quiz, long-form sales page, webinar sign-up, app store link. Brands in the same industry tend to settle on one type once it works.
7. **Tracking and tools.** Pop-ups, chat, countdown timers. They hint at how the brand converts.


## Log it so it is useful next month


A pile of links is not research. Keep one row per landing page, with these columns: brand, ad creative (a screenshot), the full URL, the page type, the offer, the date you saw it, and how long the ad has been live. Revisit monthly. A page that is gone means the test lost. A page that is still there with the same ads after three months is a winner worth learning from.


Run length is the best free signal available. Meta publishes no spend or conversion data for ordinary ads, so an ad that keeps running is the proxy for one that pays. The hooks behind those long-runners are covered in[how to analyze competitor ads for winning hooks](https://www.sprites.ai/blog/analyze-competitor-ads-winning-hooks) .


## Ground rules


- Clicking an ad costs the advertiser money. Click the ones you need, once, not repeatedly.
- Do not copy a page. Learn the structure, the order of proof and the offer logic, then write your own.
- Landing pages change. Screenshot the whole page, not only the top.

## Frequently asked questions


### How do I find the landing page of a Facebook ad?


Find the ad in the Meta Ad Library, then click its call-to-action button. It opens the landing page. Copy the full address from the browser, including the part after the question mark, because that holds the tracking tags.


### Can I see all the landing pages a competitor uses?


You can see all the ones attached to their active ads, which is most of what matters. Pages for ads that stopped running disappear from the library, so keep a log and check monthly.


### What do UTM parameters tell me about a competitor?


Sometimes the campaign name, the audience, the channel and the creative variant. Names are chosen by the advertiser, so they range from very clear to meaningless. Even a coded name shows which ad and page belong together.


### Is it legal to look at a competitor's landing pages?


Yes. Landing pages are public, and the ad libraries exist so people can see them. Do not copy their text or images, and do not click their ads in volume.


### Do competitors see that I clicked their ad?


They see a click in their analytics but not who you are. It still costs them the click, so avoid repeated clicks. A brand page in an ad library lets you see destinations without clicking.


### How often should I check competitor landing pages?


Monthly is enough for most brands, and weekly around launches and seasonal sales such as Black Friday. Compare each visit with your log to spot new pages and retired ones.
